USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the existing Section 301 tariffs in place and continue intensive talks with Beijing without a new tariff hike, a unilateral rollback, or purchase concessions ahead of a signed text. Press for a written, two-way enforcement mechanism plus structural language on IP, forced tech transfer, and agriculture market access, and only schedule a Trump–Xi summit after those chapters are closed. Leave the Huawei/Meng legal track off the bargaining table rather than trading it for a weaker commercial deal.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The dispute is not an existential threat to US interests; it is a period of usable leverage. Lists 1–3 already cover ~$250B of Chinese imports, the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25% has been deliberately held in reserve (delayed Feb 24 and again past the March 1 window), and China is still at the table after matching retaliation on ~$110B of US goods. April talks produced reported progress on text and enforcement offices, Mnuchin said the sides had “pretty much agreed” an enforcement mechanism and hoped they were near a “final round,” and Trump described an “epic” deal that was “very close” but still had “some way to go.” That is opportunity, not crisis: VIX is ~13, Michigan sentiment is back near 97, and 10-year yields have eased rather than signaling a trade-war recession. The reading is only a modest opportunity, not a clear one, because farm-belt costs are real (record soybean stocks, China buys still about a third of the pre-tariff run-rate, USDA aid already paying out billions), US industrial production has slipped ~1.7% over the window, and China’s Q1 GDP held at 6.4% with a March IP surprise of +8.5%, so Beijing is not overextended. Escalating now would risk blowing up the most constructive negotiating window since G20; conceding purchases or rolling back tariffs before enforcement and structural chapters are locked would repeat the May 2018 “trade war on hold” collapse. Negotiate without new commitments is therefore the stance that harvests leverage rather than spending it.
key_factors: Section 301 coverage still ~$250B with the List 3 10-to-25% hike held in reserve
April 2019 talks report progress on text and enforcement offices but no signed deal
US macro calm (VIX ~13, sentiment ~97) versus real but contained farm-export damage
China Q1 6.4% GDP and March IP rebound reduce the case that Beijing is desperate
Huawei/Meng extradition and Canadian detentions remain a separate legal/political overlay

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay in the April text process and keep talking without new commitments. Do not widen retaliation while the List 3 10-to-25 percent hike remains suspended, and do not lock in large purchase or enforcement concessions until Washington puts a concrete tariff-removal path on paper. Keep existing counter-tariffs as leverage; treat the Huawei/Meng track as parallel, not as something to trade away unilaterally for a commercial deal that still leaves U.S. duties in place.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The dispute is still costly but no longer at peak-escalation. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage remains about $250 billion of Chinese goods after List 3 took effect at 10 percent on 24 September 2018, and China already answered with 5–10 percent duties on about $60 billion of U.S. goods. That bite shows up in the data: U.S. goods imports from China fell from $46.3 billion in November 2018 to $34.5 billion in April 2019 (−25.6 percent), China’s Q1 2019 exports to the U.S. slipped 3.7 percent, and China’s imports from the U.S. fell 28 percent in Q1. Huawei is still under unsealed DOJ fraud/sanctions charges (28 January 2019), Meng remains in Vancouver, and Washington is pressing allies on 5G—firm-level targeting of a national champion that sits near the +0.5 China threat anchor. What keeps the reading below that anchor is the post-G20 truce: Trump delayed the List 3 hike on 24 February 2019, the 1 March deadline passed without an increase, and April talks (Liu He in Washington; 3 April timeline entry; Mnuchin on 10 April) reported progress on enforcement offices and draft text, with the U.S. even watering down subsidy demands. Q1 GDP held at 6.4 percent, March industrial production rose 8.5 percent, and stimulus has offset much of the tariff shock—so this is a managed, not existential, threat (+0.30). Escalation now would risk the very 25 percent hike and possible further lists that the delay bought time to avoid, just as domestic data are stabilizing. Full or partial rollback, or standalone purchase commitments, would be premature: U.S. officials still say some tariffs will stay, and China has historically resisted a sovereignty-eroding unilateral snapback. Negotiate—engage, explore de-escalation, make no new binding give—is the stance that matches a moderate threat and preserves leverage if the remaining gaps (tariff removal, enforcement, IP/tech transfer) do not close.

Escalation would likely revive the delayed 25% hike; unilateral purchases/rollback would surrender leverage without a matching U.S. offer
